name: Protocol
first: A named list of requirements, such as methods and properties, that a type conforms to by naming the protocol and having everything it requires.

dependsOn.why: A protocol's method requirement is written as the first line of a function, with no body.
dependsOn.whyInExample: Line 2 of `Greeter` is the first line of a function, `greet(name:)`, as line 1 of `greet` is, but with no body.

what.is: A protocol is a named list of requirements: methods and properties that a type must have. A type conforms to a protocol when it writes the protocol's name after its own, with a colon, and has everything the protocol requires.
what.afterExample: `Greeter` is a protocol with one requirement, the method `greet(name:)`. `Friendly` conforms to `Greeter`: line 4 says so, and lines 5 to 7 give `Friendly` its own `greet(name:)`.
what.problem: Code often needs to know only what a value can do, not which type it is. A protocol states what a type must be able to do, as a list of requirements, and swiftc checks that every type that conforms to it has them all.
what.how: A requirement has no body: it gives only a name, a parameter list, and a return type. Each type that conforms writes its own method, with a body. If `Friendly` had no `greet(name:)`, line 4 would not build: swiftc says that type `Friendly` does not conform to protocol `Greeter`.

when.text: Use one when several types must offer the same methods or properties, so that code can rely on them. Each type writes its own:
Don't write one for a single type that no other type has to match. Then the type's own methods are enough, as `Friendly`'s would be without `: Greeter`.

parts.name: `protocol`
parts.text: `protocol` is a keyword. On line 1 it declares a protocol, and the protocol's name, `Greeter`, comes right after it. The protocol's requirements are between the braces on lines 1 and 3.

parts.name: The requirement, on line 2
parts.text: Line 2 is a requirement: a method that every type that conforms to `Greeter` must have. A method is a function that belongs to a type. A method requirement is written as the first line of a function, with no body, so it gives only the method's name, its parameter list, and its return type.

parts.name: The conformance, `: Greeter`
parts.text: On line 4, `: Greeter` after the name `Friendly` says that `Friendly` conforms to `Greeter`. swiftc then checks that `Friendly` has everything that `Greeter` requires. A type that has the method, but does not write `: Greeter`, does not conform to `Greeter`.

parts.name: The implementation, lines 5 to 7
parts.text: Lines 5 to 7 are `Friendly`'s own `greet(name:)`. It has the name, the parameter list, and the return type of the requirement on line 2, and a body. It meets that requirement, so it is called the requirement's implementation.

steps.text: Line 9 makes a `Friendly` value, and stores it in `host`.
Line 10 calls `greet(name:)` on `host`, with the argument `"Ana"`.
`host` is a `Friendly`, so `Friendly`'s own `greet(name:)` runs, with `name` set to `"Ana"`. Line 6 returns the string "Hello, Ana".

end.text: A protocol lists what a type must have, with no bodies. `Friendly` conforms to `Greeter`, and its own `greet(name:)` is the code that runs.
